problems.description: test_list_tasks_ordered_desc_by_created_at relies on time.sleep(0.01) between inserts to establish order; timing-dependent tests are flaky and should instead inject explicit timestamps or assert on deterministic ordering.
Removing fetch_task (documented as 'used by legacy clients') is a hard breaking change; acceptable in a greenfield session but should be noted if any consumer exists outside the app.

Mechanical scan flags 'test_app.py: Classes should use PascalCase', but the new test file defines no classes (functions + fixtures only) — appears to be a false positive, not a real violation introduced by this commit.

strengths: Fixes a real correctness bug: new tasks were inserted with status 'done' instead of 'pending'.
Deletes dead code (legacy format helper, unused notification stub, alias function), reducing maintenance surface; SonarQube confirms smell count decreased by 1.
Adds a comprehensive pytest suite covering success, error (400/404), persistence, and ordering paths.
commit_reviews.summary: Clean greenfield commit that removes dead code, fixes the status-default bug, and adds solid test coverage; the 0.71 convention score is driven by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py), not by code in this diff.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-change-me' when the env var is unset, so tokens can be forged if deployed without configuration; should fail fast or generate a random per-process key.
Adds 32 functions (auth, JWT, multi-tenant scoping, schema migration) with no accompanying tests; the owner_id scoping is security-critical and untested.
_migrate_add_owner_id runs a PRAGMA/ALTER TABLE check on every init_db() call; works but is an ad-hoc shim better replaced by a versioned one-time migration.
Uses deprecated datetime.utcnow() and adds some double-blank-line spacing inconsistent with surrounding code.
JWT sub claim holds an int rather than the RFC 7519 string form, and tokens carry no revocation/blacklist path.

strengths: Correct multi-tenant data scoping: every task query filters by owner_id, preventing cross-user IDOR.
Idiomatic Flask auth: login_required decorator wiring g.user_id, proper password hashing via werkzeug.security, exp-bearing JWT.
Backward-compatible schema migration keeps the pre-auth database working across story sessions.
New code mirrors the existing single-file structure (section headers, snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE constants) and reuses the get_db()/error-dict patterns.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped, idiomatic auth + multi-tenant addition that fits the single-file baseline and scopes every task query by owner_id, though the 0.71 convention score is dragged down by pre-existing violations in files this commit never touched (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py, test_app.py — AST shows +0 classes, so the app.py PascalCase flag is not from this diff), and the hardcoded fallback secret plus absent tests are real debt.

problems.description: create_user silently fabricates a default email (f'{username}@example.com') for users who register without one; this invents data rather than leaving it nullable, and pre-existing users (email column NULL) will still trigger notifications addressed to None on task completion.

Notification trigger logic (transition-to-completed check, owner lookup, task dispatch) lives directly in the edit_task controller, mixing delivery policy with request handling; consistent with the app's flat style but pushes business rules into the view layer.

celery_config routes tasks to a 'notifications' queue, but no worker invocation, Docker/Procfile entry, or documentation is included — a default `celery -A` worker (celery queue only) would silently never consume these tasks, so the feature is inert unless an operator knows to run `-Q notifications`.
send_notification_email calls both logger.info and print(); the print duplicates logging in a task that is itself a stub email sink.

Measured convention violations (score 0.71) are largely linter false positives or pre-existing: lowercase celery_config module attributes are Celery's required config convention, and repositories.py (1 violation) is untouched by this diff while the app.py/test_app.py 'PascalCase classes' warnings reference no new classes.

strengths: Follows the existing migration pattern exactly: _migrate_add_email mirrors _migrate_add_owner_id with the same PRAGMA table_info guard.

Comprehensive notification tests cover the happy path plus dedup guard (already-completed), non-completed status changes, title-only edits, 404s, and cross-user ownership — all asserting on the mock delay call.
Proper Celery setup: config object with env-var overrides, JSON serializers, and named-queue routing via task_routes, decoupled from the Flask app.
Dedup guard sends the email only on an actual in-progress->completed transition, not on idempotent re-completions.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid integration commit that adds async notifications with thorough tests and faithful reuse of the app's migration pattern, though it hides minor debt behind fabricated default emails, controller-embedded dispatch logic, and an unprovisioned worker queue — and its low measured convention score is mostly linter noise on Celery's required lowercase config plus pre-existing violations in untouched files.

problems.description: Layering is mixed: repositories own the SQL but business preparation (password hashing, email defaulting, created_at generation) still lives in app.py, so the repository layer is a thin SQL shell rather than a full domain boundary. Acceptable at this scale, but a service layer would be the cleaner home.
Refactor is partial: init_db and _migrate_add_email still execute raw SQL directly in app.py, leaving two coexisting data-access styles in the same module.

BaseRepository.insert/update_fields build SQL via f-strings from dict keys; safe because keys are internal constants (never user input), but column/type errors surface only at runtime rather than via explicit statements.

The measured 0.71 convention score is repo-wide and driven by pre-existing violations in files untouched by this diff (celery_config.py, notifications.py, test_app.py, plus a pre-existing app.py class rule); SonarQube delta of +0 smells indicates this commit adds no new violations.

strengths: Dependency-injects the existing get_db factory rather than importing a connection, preserving late resolution of DATABASE for tests and callers — behavior explicitly documented in the commit.
Removes ~60 lines of duplicated per-function SQL from app.py and centralizes table access in dedicated repository classes.
Preserves all public function signatures (create_user, get_user_by_id, get_task, etc.), so route handlers and callers are unaffected by the refactor.
Adds zero new SonarQube issues (bugs, smells, cognitive complexity, duplication all +0) and reduces code duplication by consolidating shared CRUD.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, low-risk repository-pattern refactor that injects the existing get_db factory, preserves caller-facing signatures, and cuts ~60 lines of duplicated SQL with no new SonarQube issues — the 0.71 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in unrelated files, not this commit.

problems.description: Rate limiting introduces a hard runtime/test dependency on Redis at redis://localhost:6379/1; the app and the full test suite (autouse fixture calls flushdb) now fail without external infra that the app previously did not require, even though RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI is env-overridable.

SonarQube cognitive complexity +22 comes from the nested cursor/limit validation block in list_tasks plus the two-branch rate_limit_key; the parsing could be extracted into a helper to keep the route thin.

GET /tasks response shape changes from a bare list to {data, next_cursor, total} and get_tasks() returns a 3-tuple instead of a list — a breaking API/contract change; internally fine (single caller), but callers outside the story would break.
Every page issues an extra COUNT(*) via count_for_owner plus a cursor lookup query; negligible at story scale but a per-request cost worth noting.
A stale/invalid cursor silently returns an empty page from list_for_owner rather than surfacing an error, which could be mistaken for end-of-results by a client.

strengths: Keyset pagination with (created_at, id) tuple ordering keeps ties on created_at deterministic and produces a proper next_cursor without OFFSET drift.
Rate limiting keys by authenticated user (decoding JWT ahead of login_required) with IP fallback, so it applies uniformly to unauthenticated endpoints like /auth/login — a sound anti-abuse default.
New code follows existing patterns: pagination/count live in TaskRepository, routing stays thin, and SECRET_KEY/JWT_ALGORITHM are reused rather than re-parsed.
Constants (DEFAULT_PAGE_LIMIT, MAX_PAGE_LIMIT, RATE_LIMIT) are UPPER_CASE and env-configurable; limits are validated and clamped (400 on bad input).
Non-obvious decisions are documented (rate_limit_key ordering rationale, cursor ordering semantics), and tests were updated for the new envelope plus an isolation fixture.
The new code itself is convention-clean: snake_case functions, PascalCase imported class, UPPER_CASE module constants, type hints on signatures.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-engineered commit that cleanly adds pagination and user-aware rate limiting while respecting the repository pattern and JWT conventions, but it introduces real technical debt via a hard Redis dependency for the app and test suite — and its own code is convention-clean (≈0.85), so the measured 0.71 codebase convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notifications.py) rather than anything this diff adds.

compounding_issues: Seed inserted tasks with status 'done' while returning 'pending' — Session 1 caught and corrected it, so it did not propagate, but it was a latent inconsistency in the baseline.
Session 2's owner_id migration backfills no owner for pre-existing tasks, leaving seed data permanently invisible to all users (they are owned by nobody).
Session 5's tests depend on a live Redis instance and hardcode redis://localhost:6379/1, and RATE_LIMIT=100/min makes rate-limit tests iterate 100 requests each — slow and environment-coupled.
Celery worker is never actually run in-story; async delivery is only verified via mock.delay and a direct task call, so end-to-end delivery is unproven.
Default SECRET_KEY='dev-secret-change-me' persisted through all 5 sessions as a production-hygiene smell.
key_decisions: Session 1 sanitized the seed (fixed the status bug, deleted dead helpers) and established a 13-test baseline before adding features.

Session 2 introduced a per-user ownership model (Task.owner_id) plus a reusable migration helper (_migrate_add_owner_id) that Session 3 replicated for email — the ownership scoping shaped every later SQL WHERE clause.

Session 4's Repository pattern with get_db factory injection was the pivotal architecture move: Session 5's cursor pagination (list_for_owner with cursor/limit, count_for_owner) and the 'tasks unchanged' refactor proof depended on it.

Session 5 keyed the rate limiter by JWT-decoded user (decoding ahead of login_required) so auth endpoints are covered too, and implemented cursor pagination on the (created_at, id) tuple for deterministic tie-break ordering.
Session 3 triggered notifications only on the completed-transition edge (new_status=='completed' and previous != completed), avoiding duplicate sends.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically. Session 1 repaired the defective seed, then tests grew 13→29→37→37→49 across the story with code size staying compact (app.py 130→295 lines). Session 4 was a clean pure refactor — app.py shrank from 274 to 231 lines, test_app.py untouched, all tests still green. Session 5 delivered the most complex behavior (rate limiting + cursor pagination) with the strongest test suite, covering cross-user cursor isolation, per-user and per-IP bucket separation, Retry-After headers, and 429 handling. Tool usage (18→19→29→21→42 steps) tracked increasing session complexity. The only flat segment is S3→S4 test count, which is expected from a constraint that prohibited test modifications during the refactor.
story_review.summary: An unusually coherent, self-reinforcing 5-session arc where the Session 2 ownership model and Session 4 repository abstraction were decisions that made Session 5's cross-cutting features land cleanly, with quality rising steadily and all 49 tests passing at the end.
